title: Website Templates: 7 Tests Before You Buy the Pretty Demo
seoTitle: Website Templates: 7 Checks Before You Buy | CodeMax
description: Choose a website template around your content, mobile layout and customer journey. Use these seven practical checks before committing to a design.
author: CodeMax
html:
A website template can shorten the path to a finished small business website. But a polished demo is usually filled with carefully selected photographs, short headlines and ideal sample content. Your real services may not fit those assumptions. Before buying a template, test it with the information your customers actually need.

1. Replace the hero with your own message

Write one sentence explaining what you do, who you help and where you operate. Put it into the proposed layout without cutting essential meaning to match the demo. If a clear sentence becomes tiny or overlaps a button, the design needs adjustment. The first screen should remain understandable when the photograph changes.

For example, a Melbourne consultant may need to explain both a service and the type of business it suits. A two-word fashion headline is unlikely to do that job. Choose a layout that makes the useful information easy to read instead of forcing your business into a visual style.

2. Try your longest service name on mobile

Use a narrow screen and your longest realistic headings, menu labels and button text. Check that words wrap naturally, links stay readable and visitors can move through the page without horizontal scrolling. Test a real phone as well as the browser preview when possible.

Also look at the page after increasing text size. A template that only works with a precise headline length will create repeated editing problems. Responsive web design needs to accommodate real content, not just shrink an attractive desktop screenshot.

3. Follow one complete customer task

Choose a task such as finding a suitable service and requesting a callback. Begin on the homepage, find the supporting information and reach the contact step. Note any missing explanations or repeated clicks. A template with many impressive sections can still leave a simple journey unfinished.

Check the empty, error and confirmation states too. What does a visitor see when a required field is missing? Where do they go after submitting? These details should be part of the implementation scope, even if the template demonstration omits them.

4. Check the images you can actually supply

Replace wide landscape photography with your available images. Check whether important details disappear when the mobile crop changes. If the layout needs ten large professional photographs and you have two, decide whether to commission more or simplify the design.

Record which demo assets are included and which require separate licences. Do not publish sample customer logos, testimonials or project photographs as though they represent your business. Use only material you have permission to use and claims you can support.

5. Test basic accessibility

Use the keyboard to move through the navigation and controls. Confirm that you can see where focus is and that a mouse is not required for an essential action. Check text contrast and whether form labels remain visible. W3C's preliminary checks are a useful starting point, although passing them is not a full accessibility assessment.

6. Ask what controls search presentation

Confirm that each page can have a descriptive title and useful content headings. Ask how canonical URLs, redirects and the sitemap will be handled in the finished site. Google advises concise, descriptive page titles; repeating a list of keywords in every title is not a substitute for clear content.

7. Rehearse a routine edit

Have the future editor change an image and update a paragraph. Check whether the layout survives. Then list the template price, required add-ons, setup work and ongoing support separately. The strongest choice is the template that supports your content and customer tasks with a manageable amount of work.
